Valley of Baca
BAY-kuh
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Baca, "weeping" (or a balsam tree of dry places); the valley of weeping that the pilgrim turns into a well of springs.

📖 Biblical Definition

The valley of Baca, meaning "weeping" (or named for balsam trees that grow in arid ground), appears in the great pilgrim psalm as an image of the hard and sorrowful places through which the people of God pass on their way to Zion. "Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them. Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools" (Psa 84:5-6). The pilgrims, set on going up to the house of God, do not avoid the valley of weeping but pass through it — and as they go, they make it a well, turning the place of tears into a source of refreshment, while the rain of heaven fills the pools. "They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God" (Psa 84:7). The valley of Baca stands in the dictionary as the valley of weeping made a well, a picture of the believer's pilgrimage through sorrow: those whose strength is in God do not merely endure the hard places but transform them, digging wells of refreshment in the desert of grief, and going from strength to strength until they appear before God in Zion.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The "valley of weeping" in Psalm 84:6 that pilgrims, whose strength is in God, turn into a well of springs as they journey to Zion; a picture of transforming sorrow into refreshment on the way to God.

VALLEY OF BACA, proper noun. "Weeping"; an image of sorrow in the pilgrim psalm.

Through which those whose strength is in God pass on the way to Zion.

Which the pilgrims "make a well" — turning weeping into refreshment (Psa 84:6).

On the way to appearing before God in Zion, from strength to strength (Psa 84:7).

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Baca needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that the pilgrim whose strength is in God turns the valley of weeping into a well, transforming sorrow into refreshment on the way to Zion.

expand to see more

Sorrow-avoided correction. The natural heart seeks a path to God that skirts all weeping. The pilgrim psalm assumes the valley of Baca lies on the road to Zion, and blesses those who pass through it. The dictionary holds that the way to glory runs through tribulation (Acts 14:22); the believer is not promised exemption from the valley of weeping but the strength to pass through it, and even to make it a well of refreshment for himself and others.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the transformation of sorrow by faith. Those whose strength is in God do not merely endure the valley of weeping; they make it a well, and heaven's rain fills the pools. The dictionary commends this hope: the believer's light affliction works a far more exceeding weight of glory (2 Cor 4:17), and faith digs wells in the desert of grief, going from strength to strength until it appears before God in Zion.
